kernelIdea: f: S → T assigns to every s ∈ S exactly one f(s) ∈ T. Three conditions: totality, well-definedness, and codomain. S is the domain, T the codomain.

kernels.l1: A good machine gives every child exactly one cubby. Not none, and not two.
kernels.l2: A machine takes each thing on the first list and sends it to exactly one thing on the second list. Nothing gets skipped, and nothing gets sent to two places.
kernels.l3: A function f from S to T gives every element of S exactly one partner in T. Three things must hold: nothing in S is skipped, nothing gets two answers, and every answer lands inside T.
kernels.l4: A function assigns to every element of its starting collection exactly one element of a second, declared collection. Three conditions: every input is used, no input gets two outputs, and every output lands where you said it would.
kernels.l5: A function is a rule that is total on its domain, single-valued, and lands inside its declared codomain; changing the domain or codomain changes the function.
kernels.l6: A function f: S → T assigns to every element of S exactly one element of T. Three conditions do the work: every input is used, no input gets two outputs, and every output lands in T. The vertical line test is a picture of the second one, not the definition.
kernels.l7: A function f: S → T assigns to each element of its domain exactly one element of its codomain — totality, well-definedness, and codomain membership. The domain and codomain are part of the function, not annotations on it.
kernels.l8: A function is a subset f ⊆ S × T such that each s ∈ S is the first coordinate of exactly one pair; domain and codomain are data, and "range" is ambiguous between image and codomain.

kernel: f: S → T assigns to every s ∈ S exactly one f(s) ∈ T. Three conditions: totality (everything gets sent), well-definedness (one output each), and codomain (outputs land in T). S is the domain, T the codomain.
objectives: Test a rule against the three conditions
Give a non-example of each failure
